messages.author: 64dd3e60f9213f7d
messages.subject: A foundational question
parts:
Hi all,

I have a somewhat foundational question:

If it is true that (i) inferential statistics serves to make inferences from the sample (the corpus in the case of corpus linguistics) to the population (language in the case of linguistics) and that (ii) that very population changes any second (because people receive and produce language massively and incessantly), how can those be countered who contend that, in the field of linguistics, making inferences from the sample to the population is fruitless because that population is in a constant flux?

Thanks in advance for any thoughtful pointer.

Best
Chris

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] A foundational question
parts:
by pointing out that one is doing a SYNCHRONIC study where the object
of study is the population at a particular point in time (namely the
point in time the sample is representative for as opposed to a
diachronic one where the focus is precisely the flux you mention?

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] A foundational question
parts:
This "synchronic" aspect of the study is _highly_ frequent in other disciplines. Take any survey of opinion, market evolution studies, etc. Customers choices and opinions vary constantly, yet they are studied using descriptive and also inferential statistics. The same could be said about less fast changing objects of study (such as characteristics of species, also in constant evolution/flux).  

Your population is not "language", but that particular language at the time, by the group studied, etc. Same could be said of consumers' habits, they are not a study of all consumers' habits in general, but for x product at t time. 

Irene Checa-Garcia.
